newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU steps up pressure on Telefonica, Unisource deal.
newsitem.headline: EU steps up pressure on Telefonica, Unisource deal.

text.p: The European Commission has stepped up its warnings to Spain that it will not clear the participation of Telefonica in telecommunications alliance Unisource unless the Spanish telecoms market opens up to free competition.
The move comes as the clock is ticking for a global telecoms accord under the World Trade Organisation, which negotiators hope to conclude early in 1997.
Spain is the only large EU country that has not yet committed itself to open all telecoms markets to competition by January 1, 1998.

Commission sources said on Monday that unless the Spanish government agreed quickly to respect the deadline, Telefonica de Espana SA could be left out of the alliance formed with telecoms partners in Sweden, the Netherlands and Switzerland.
"We are still waiting for a definitive answer on the January, 1 1998 deadline," one source said on the condition of anonymity.
"We can't exclude that we may give the green light to the three other partners and not to Telefonica," the source added.
In principle, Spain has the right under EU legislation to delay by up to five years scrapping the monopoly of partly state-owned Telefonica.
But the Commission has made it crystal clear for more than a year that Spain must renounce the delay if it wants clearance of Unisource.

Unisource International NV is an agreement between Dutch PTT, Telia AB of Sweden and Swiss Telecom PTT -- who in the early 90s agreed to pool efforts in mainly value-added telecom services -- on the one hand and Telefonica on the other hand.
The Spanish telecoms operator owns 25 percent of Unisource.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert hinted last week that his patience with Spain was running out.
"If things don't move rapidly we risk having a serious conflict," Van Miert told the European Parliament's Economic and Monetary Affairs Committee on Thursday.
The Commission first publicly queried the Unisource deal in March 1995 following the four partners' apparent unwillingness to submit their alliance for EU clearance.
It also asked to be notified of a subsequent alliance with U.S. telecoms giant AT&T Corp called Uniworld.

The Commission's effort to open up Spain's market is similar to the approach it used when deciding whether to clear the Atlas joint venture between Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom and their global alliance with Sprint Corp.
The Commission cleared that deal last July after years of hard bargaining.
The Spanish government has proposed to renounce only part of the extra time it won during hard-fought EU negotiations on telecoms deregulation.
But the Commission believes that Telefonica, Europe's fifth largest operator, should be given the same treatment as its French and German rivals.
The EU is also under pressure from the United States to create a fully liberalised EU telecoms market in 1998.
The United States and the Union agreed in June, in Lyon, France, to aim to conclude a telecommunications agreement by February 15, 1997.
